"I like Honeycomb a lot and we're dependent on it for parts of our orchestrator. It's great; it accelerates investigations." However, even with Honeycomb they sit on "an absolute mountain of telemetry data" in logs, metrics, and Honeycomb trace indices. Having the data in a graph doesn't mean a solution is near, and drilling down still takes time.

Integrating information across data sources is a big open challenge. In any given incident the team is looking at Honeycomb traces, OpenSearch for system logs, and Prometheus metrics in a VictoriaMetrics cluster. No single telemetry tool connects these effectively. An LLM agent given tool calls for each source, including Honeycomb's MCP server, can generate integrated hypotheses.

Commenter suggests Honeycomb's AI observability post could be retitled "how to 10x your observability costs": you still need alerts and graphs to know latency is spiking before prompting, and the extra compute for anomaly detection and sub-second queries means spending much more. "I can totally see why this is great for honeycomb though, they're going to make bank."

Commenter calls Honeycomb's AI observability article "a thinly veiled marketing promo" and says lines like "Honeycomb's entire modus operandi is predicated on fast feedback loops... built for the future" are "as subtle as a sledgehammer to the forehead."

Commenter notes Honeycomb's agent 'zero-shot' example was the same scenario Honeycomb uses in its demos, so the solution may have been in the training data. They say a contrived example was needed to show the tool can generalize before declaring the end of observability.

Commenter disputes the claim that Honeycomb "led the way for OpenTelemetry." OTel came from merging OpenCensus (Google) and OpenTracing (LightStep). Honeycomb made valuable code and community contributions and championed adoption, but was "very far from 'leading the way'."
Commenter points out that Honeycomb blogged about an LLM-driven latency analysis that was only an internal demo, and Datadog launched a shipping product in the same space (Bits AI SRE) a day later.

On Honeycomb's post about building LLM product features: "I think this may be the best thing I've read about real-world prompt engineering - there's SO MUCH hard earned knowledge in here. The description of how they're handling the threat of prompt injection was particularly smart."
Commenter says Honeycomb's LLM article reads like a list of everything everybody is already talking about, while skipping the hard part of "how to make a profit."

Reader praises Honeycomb's Kafka scaling write-up as excellent, explaining Kafka, their specific use of it, and the history of their implementation in plain language: "whoever wrote this knows their Ops." Another calls it an awesome "warts and all" account, more useful than typical "we switched to X and saved Y%" marketing posts.

Commenter questions Honeycomb staying on self-packaged Kafka 0.10.0 until July 2019, saying they missed many bug fixes. In their own experience, moving past 0.11.x cut recovery after an unclean shutdown from about two hours to about 10 minutes.

Commenter says Honeycomb's 24–48 hour buffer to guard against bugs corrupting customer data is small. They have used much larger buffers because some bugs, especially missing data, can lurk unnoticed for a long time.

Operator running hundreds of Kafka clusters at tens of millions of messages/sec says they never needed the CPU and network/disk throughput Honeycomb describes. They use fewer cores but ~248GB memory per broker and suggest Honeycomb's broker sizing may not have been ideal for the workload.

Commenter says Honeycomb's Kafka post likely counts vCPUs as cores. On x86 AWS a vCPU is a hyperthread, while on Graviton2 it is a full core, so Intel looks less bad than presented (10 Intel cores vs 16 Graviton, not 20). The arm64 cost savings still hold.
